salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.confidence_note: The counts of families, landowners, hectares and the rupee amounts all come from the Bank's own completion report, which also carries the impact evaluation's findings on water, floor allotment and theft at the Salem flats. The Independent Evaluation Group reviewed that report rather than going into the field, so the lender is the only source. No outside record of the Salem resettlement was found: Indian Kanoon holds one order naming the project's Chennai unit (V. Anandaraj, W.P.No.16873 of 2018, Madras High Court, 6 August 2018, where the Chief Engineer, Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project, Project Implementation Unit TNUDP-III was the second respondent and a patta holder asked for land taken for East Coast Road to be struck off his revenue record) and a further run of Madras High Court compensation disputes against the Special Deputy Collector (Land Acquisition), Highways Department, TNUDP-III, but the corridors in them - East Coast Road six-laning at Palavakkam, the Porur grade separator, the Arumbakkam grade separators - are not among the five Chennai roads the completion report says the loan financed, so none of them can be attributed to the Bank-financed works. What the re-reading of the completion report does establish is that the roads it financed in Chennai are named in its own annexes (MKT Road, Madhervedu Road, Taramani Link Road, Ariyalur-Vilangadupakkam and Koladi Road), that the Chennai urban transport sub-component was cut from 21 proposed sub-projects to five in the August 2009 restructuring and from US$147.5 million to US$34 million because of land acquisition problems, and that the only Salem sub-project in the project's sub-project list is the Salem river improvement scheme on the Thirumanimuthar River. Nothing opened says whether the 65 families were given title to their flats.
corrections: The card says of the lender's role that the loan 'financed 110 sub-projects under the urban investment component as well as the Chennai urban transport sub-component' without recording how far that sub-component shrank. The completion report (ICR00003125, 30 September 2014, section 1.7 and p.4) states that 21 urban transport sub-projects were proposed at the start, that at mid-term review only five road sub-projects were judged adequately prepared and were retained for Bank financing in the August 2009 restructuring, and that the sub-component fell from US$147.5 million to US$34 million because of land acquisition issues that arose in the first stages of implementation. The scale of that cut is the project's largest single land-acquisition fact and the card does not carry it.

The card's confidence note says the report 'does not say where in Salem the families were moved from or to'. The report's annexes do narrow the first half: the beneficiary-survey table of surveyed sub-projects lists one Salem sub-project, 'River Improvement', and Annex 2 describes it as improvements to the Thirumanimuthar River over a 2,800 m stretch, regularising the cross-section of the Vellakuttai Oodai and three bridges. Since the report also says resettlement was involved in only one of the 110 urban investment sub-projects and that that one town was Salem, the 65 squatter families were on the Thirumanimuthar works. The report does not state this in one sentence, so it is an inference from two annexes and not a document reading.

The report records a figure the card omits: the project 'facilitated the inclusion of 400 non-title holders for R&R assistance' (ICR00003125, social safeguards passage). The card carries 337 non-title holders affected in Chennai and no figure for non-title holders actually assisted.

The Chennai roads the loan financed are named, against the card's silence on them: the completion report's economic analysis annex gives the five CMDA roads as MKT Road, Madhervedu Road, Taramani Link Road, Ariyalur-Vilangadupakkam and Koladi Road, 34.80 km in all with five foot-over bridges. This matters because the Madras High Court land-acquisition cases that carry the TNUDP-III name are on other corridors.
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.what_the_outside_source_settles: Nothing about the Salem families. The one outside document that names the project (Madras High Court, V. Anandaraj v. The Tahsildar, Sholinganallur and the Chief Engineer, TNUDP-III, W.P.No.16873 of 2018, order of 6 August 2018) settles only that the project's Chennai implementation unit was still a respondent in revenue disputes over land it had taken four years after the loan closed, and that in that case the patta for land taken for East Coast Road still stood in the name of a man who was neither owner nor occupier; the court directed his representation of 27 February 2018 to be decided in eight weeks.
salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether the 65 Salem families received title to their flats in December 2014 or at all; whether the water, floor-allotment and theft findings at the Salem flats were acted on; whether the delays in paying compensation the lender reports happened as described; and whether any of the TNUDP-III compensation litigation in Madras High Court touches the five Bank-financed Chennai roads. The East Coast Road, Porur and Arumbakkam acquisitions carry the project's name through its Highways Department implementation unit but are not among the five roads the completion report says the Bank paid for.

ZambiaLII's whole holding on the place name is 69 documents, of which five are judgments: two Zambia Revenue Authority customs appeals (2002, 2012), a road carriage negligence case (2012), a trade mark case (2024) and a 2003 criminal appeal; none concerns the border post works, the council or the traders, and the rest are statutory instruments and gazettes that match on the place name alone. uganda-ert2-grid-compensation.confidence_note: The breach of the Bank's resettlement policy is stated in the World Bank's own completion report and in the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. Outside the lender, the Ministry of Finance's Budget Monitoring and Accountability Unit, which monitors the government's own spending, reported in June 2014 - the month after the Bank downgraded the safeguards rating - that every one of the 34 grid extension projects it monitored had problems implementing its resettlement action plan, and that the land compensation problems included locals refusing to let contractors 'erect poles in their compounds, and cut their trees before being compensated', with some people threatening to sue the Rural Electrification Agency for entering their land before compensation. Its recommendation was that the agency deal with the resettlement action plan before projects start. Eight of the lines it names are lines the completion report lists as built under this credit. The paper does not say line by line which projects the compensation failures were on, and its one named instance is at Hamurwa trading centre on the Kabale-Kisoro line, which is not one of this credit's lines; nor does it or any other document found give a number of people affected or paid. The Ugandan judgment route produced four Rural Electrification Agency cases, including an Electricity Disputes Tribunal award for trespass and destroyed trees, but their works are dated 2008, 2019 and 2019/2020 - before this credit started or after it closed - so none of them records this credit's harm.

uganda-ert2-grid-compensation.what_it_does_not_settle: How many people were owed compensation, how many were paid, how much, or on which line. zambia-2004-wage-freeze-teachers.confidence_note: The harm is on the record outside the lender, in Zambian and regional press of 2004 and in the words of Zambia's own ministers. The Mail & Guardian and Inter Press Service carried the same dispatch by Zarina Geloo from Lusaka on 16 February 2004: the finance minister, Ng'andu Magande, announced in the budget of 6 February a rise in pay-as-you-earn tax to up to 40 per cent and a wage freeze on more than 120,000 public service workers, having said in a pre-budget television interview a week earlier that he would not raise taxes, and said the government 'had no option' but to get back on the Poverty Reduction Growth Facility by June; the Zambia Congress of Trade Unions president, Leonard Hikaumba, called a national protest for 18 February outside parliament, and the Federation of Free Trade Unions president, Joyce Nonde, demanded that the government publish the debt-relief conditions. The Times of Zambia of 10 February 2004 reported public service unions meeting in Lusaka to contest the freeze and President Mwanawasa and Magande telling them it was aimed at getting back onto the IMF programme after Zambia missed the debt-relief completion point in December 2003. The Times of Ndola of 19 February 2004 reported that the strike went ahead, that the Congress of Trade Unions secretary-general Sylvester Tembo put the public-sector turnout at 90 per cent and that about 500,000 workers marched to parliament. On the teachers, the Times of Zambia of 20 October 2004 reported the education minister, Andrew Mulenga, asking for the IMF's policies to be relaxed, saying the country needed more teachers but had to follow those policies to reach the completion point, and asking to be allowed to spend more than 8.1 per cent of GDP on personal emoluments; the same report gives the shortage as about 9,000 teachers against 12,000 trained teachers who could not be put on the payroll. What stays contested is the cause, and now from both sides: the IMF says its policies never barred the hiring of teachers, and on 3 February 2004 the education ministry's own press officer, Michael Katowa, denied that the failure to deploy 9,000 teachers was down to World Bank and IMF conditionalities, saying 'The government has not deployed the teachers because there are no funds'. Two of the Zambian press items were read in the Southern Africa Documentation and Cooperation Centre's republication rather than on the newspapers' own pages, which no longer carry 2004.

field_changes.community: Zambia's 2004 budget, presented on 6 February by finance minister Ng'andu Magande, raised pay-as-you-earn tax to up to 40 per cent and froze the wages of more than 120,000 public service workers; a week earlier Magande had said on national television that he would not raise taxes (Mail & Guardian and Inter Press Service, 16 February 2004). Public service unions met in Lusaka to contest the freeze and President Mwanawasa and Magande told them it was meant to get Zambia back onto the IMF programme after the country missed the debt-relief completion point in December 2003, which the government blamed on a budget overrun caused in part by the previous year's wage increments (The Times of Zambia, 10 February 2004). On the teachers, the education minister Andrew Mulenga said in October 2004 that Zambia needed more teachers but had to follow IMF policies to reach the completion point, and asked to be allowed to spend more than 8.1 per cent of GDP on personal emoluments; the same report gives a shortage of about 9,000 teachers against 12,000 trained teachers who could not be put on the payroll (The Times of Zambia, 20 October 2004). Nine months earlier the education ministry's press officer, Michael Katowa, had denied that the 9,000 undeployed teachers were a consequence of World Bank and IMF conditionalities, saying there were no funds for salaries and that teachers already in post would have to double their workload (IRIN, 3 February 2004). Teachers on the Copperbelt struck in September 2004 over a 40 per cent housing allowance the government owed them, which the Ministry of Education called illegal (The Times of Zambia, 14 September 2004).
field_changes.outcome: Workers struck against the tax rise and wage cap: the Congress of Trade Unions secretary-general Sylvester Tembo put the public-sector turnout at 90 per cent and about 500,000 workers marched to parliament on 18 February 2004, where opposition members moved for a poverty line and a minimum wage (The Times of Ndola and SouthScan, 19 February 2004). The Netherlands gave K48 billion, about US$10 million, towards hiring teachers. It did not produce the 7,000 posts the unions had been promised: in December 2004 the education minister said only 1,000 teachers would be given posts at the start of the 2005 academic year, rural areas first, and the Zambia National Union of Teachers said the government had reneged on recruiting all 7,000 in January, its director of international affairs Joel Kamoko warning that teachers long out of work would need retraining (IRIN, 7 December 2004).

corrections: The card's outcome says 'The Netherlands gave $10 million to pay off retiring teachers so about 7,000 could be replaced (IMF letter)'. That is the plan, not the result. On 7 December 2004 the education minister said that of the 7,000, only 1,000 teachers would be given posts at the start of the 2005 academic year, and the Zambia National Union of Teachers accused the government of reneging on a guarantee to recruit all 7,000 in January (IRIN, 7 December 2004). The Dutch money is also described there as being for employing teachers, rural areas first, not for paying off retiring ones.

The card's conditions field says the wage freeze is listed among austerity measures 'without naming it as a specific IMF or World Bank condition'. The press of February 2004 goes further than that without closing it: Magande tied the freeze to getting back onto the Poverty Reduction Growth Facility by June, and Mwanawasa and Magande told the unions the same thing in person. The Zambian government presented the freeze as a condition of returning to the programme; whether the IMF required it is a separate question the IMF answers in the negative.

The card's community field gives the tax rise as hitting 'about 495,000 workers (IRIN 2005)'. The February 2004 dispatch gives two different denominators that should sit beside it: the freeze covered more than 120,000 public service workers, and the Federation of Free Trade Unions president put the number of workers being asked to subsidise 10 million Zambians at 400,000.

A harm the card does not carry at all: teachers on the Copperbelt struck in September 2004 over a 40 per cent housing allowance the government owed them, and the Ministry of Education's response was that the strike was illegal and that there was no dispute with any teachers' union (The Times of Zambia, 14 September 2004). The housing allowance is the same allowance the card's lender field names as part of the unbudgeted pay rise behind the 2003 wage cap.
zambia-2004-wage-freeze-teachers.what_the_outside_source_settles: That the wage freeze and the tax rise were imposed, when, on how many workers and by whom; that public workers struck against them and about 500,000 marched on parliament; that the government itself told the unions the freeze was for getting back onto the IMF programme; and that the education minister, in the national press, gave the shortage as about 9,000 teachers against 12,000 trained teachers who could not be paid, and asked the IMF to relax the ceiling so he could hire. The card's harm no longer rests on Oxfam's reading of the lender or on the lender's own account of itself.
zambia-2004-wage-freeze-teachers.what_it_does_not_settle: Whether the ceiling was an IMF requirement. Zambia's education ministry said in February 2004 that it was not, and its minister said in October 2004 that it was; the IMF says its policies at no time barred the hiring of teachers. The press also does not establish the teachers' union claim in the card that some rural pupils saw no teacher during 2004, and it gives no count of how many of the 12,000 were eventually paid. Two of the three Times of Zambia items were read in a third party's republication, which reproduces the text and names the paper and the date but is not the newspaper's own page.
